attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the sprite’s name in the mySprite.setPosition(x, y), and update the x and y parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you format a sprite’s name in camelCase?

❓ Which argument moves the sprite left and right on the screen? Which argument moves the sprite up and down on the screen? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that camelCase replaces spaces in text with capital letters.

💡 As needed, the ninja can toggle back to blocks to use the visual coordinate grid to help them place a sprite in their desired location.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding a sprite to tell about the different seasons!


Notice the code comments that are already in the editor: // set up and // sprite code.  


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath the comment // sprite code. 

Click the palette to select a sprite. Replace mySprite by typing a new sprite name using camelCase. Give the sprite a simple name that describes what it is, such as heroSprite.


Then, set the sprite’s position by opening Sprites and dragging [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the sprite. Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name. Update the x (0-160) and y (0-120) parameters so that the sprite appears near the bottom of the screen.


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace mySprite with the sprite’s name in mySprite.setBounceOnWall(on)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What value might you set the sprite’s velocity x (vx) to?

❓ What other properties do you recognize from the code completion tool? Which block have you noticed them in before?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out the connection between the list of properties in the code completion tool, and the drop down menu found in the [set sprite [x]] block. By using the dot operator ., the ninja can easily assign a wide variety of properties (including x, y, vx, vy, ax, ay, etc.) to a sprite.

💡 Remind the ninja that the default Boolean argument, true, in the setBounceOnWall function turns the effect on when the project starts.
steps.instructions:
Code the sprite to move horizontally and bounce on the edges of the screen!


On a line below the sprite’s existing code, type the name of the sprite, from the previous step, followed by a dot operator .


When the code completion tool appears, find and select the vx property to add it to the end of the sprite name in the code editor. Type = 45 to set the sprite’s vx to 45 pixels per second. The code will look like heroSprite.vx = 45 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) bounce on wall (true)] onto a blank line underneath the code that sets the sprite’s vx. Replace mySprite with the name of the sprite. Keep the default argument set to true, so that the bounce on walls effect is turned on when the project starts.


Click ▶ to see the sprite move horizontally on its own and bounce on the edges of the screen! Test out different values to make the sprite move faster or slower.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create 3 sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the project gets to a comment in the code? How does it know to skip it?

❓ What kind of title might be helpful to use in a comment?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that using two slashes // tells the project to skip over the following text and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when describing comments. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Add code comments to organize the code for additional scenes in the project!


Underneath the code that sets the sprite to bounce on walls, press Enter on the keyboard 2 times to add 2 blank lines. Type // scene 1 on the blank line. In JavaScript, // signals a code comment and the text that follows will appear in green. This text will be skipped over when the project is run.


Repeat this process by pressing Enter 2 more times, then typing // scene 2 on the blank line.


Repeat the process a third time by pressing Enter twice, then typing // scene 3 on the blank line.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type quotation marks around the string inside the parentheses of each game.splash(text)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it useful to use code comments to separate code that appears multiple times in a project?

❓ What might happen in each of the different scenes?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they will need to add quotation marks around the string argument in the game.splash(null) code, in order for the project to run correctly.

💡 Point out to the ninja that code comments help coders to organize their code. Help them make a connection to the way functions help separate out chunks of code into different containers. Comments create short titles for each section of code and help create more space visually, so that coders can better understand the project and identify where additional code should be placed. In this project, the code validation is specifically looking for 5 instances of //.
steps.instructions:
Splash a title on the screen to show when each scene changes!


Open Game and drag [splash (title)] onto a blank line underneath the // set up comment. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

game.splash(null)

Replace null with a project title by typing a string in quotation marks inside the parentheses. 


Add additional splash screens under each of the scene comments. Replace null by typing the name of a different season in quotation marks inside the parentheses. 


Remember to include quotation marks when typing a string, otherwise the code will not be able to run!


Click ▶ to see splash screens appear on the screen to indicate different scenes in the project!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click the palette to select background images for each scene?
steps.instructions:
Add background images that show a different season in each scene!


Open Scene and drag [set background img to (img)] underneath the splash screen code for all 3 scenes. 


Click the palette to choose a background image from the Gallery that represents each of the 3 seasons. 


Click ▶ to see the background change after each splash screen appears!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update both parameters in each game.showLongText(string, layout)?
steps.instructions:
Add dialog boxes to tell something about the season in each scene!


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] onto a blank line underneath the background image code for all 3 scenes. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

game.showLongText(null, DialogLayout.Bottom)

The showLongText function takes two parameters: string and layout. In the parentheses, highlight the first argument, null, and replace it with a string in quotation marks that tells something about the first season. Then, update the second parameter by deleting .Bottom, retyping . and selecting a new screen position from the code completion tool. 



Repeat this process for the other 2 scenes, adding a string in quotation marks about the season, then updating the position of the dialog box.


Click ▶ to see a message about each season appear in dialog boxes as the background changes!

steps.hints:
❓ Did you choose an effect and update the parameters of each effects.blizzard.startScreenEffect

(duration, particlesPerSecond)?
steps.instructions:
Code different screen effects for each of the seasons!


Open Scene and drag [start screen (effect) effect] onto a blank line underneath the dialog box code for all 3 scenes. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

effects.blizzard.startScreenEffect()

Change the effect by deleting .blizzard and retyping . after effects to open the code completion tool of possible effects. Scroll down the list to the properties, then select one that matches the theme of the season.


The startScreenEffect function takes 2 parameters: duration and particlesPerSecond. Inside the parentheses, fill in the 2 parameters with number arguments, separated by commas, to customize the screen effect. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter.


Repeat this process for the other 2 scenes, updating the effect property and both the duration and particlesPerSecond parameters.


Click ▶ to see screen effects appear for each season!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a pause(ms) to scene 1 and scene 2?
steps.instructions:
Oh no! All 3 screen effects appeared at the same time at the end of the project. Add a pause between scenes to fix this bug.


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] onto a blank line underneath the screen effect code for the first and second scene. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

pause(100)

Update the parameter by replacing 100 with the same argument used to set the duration of the screen effect. Repeat this for both the first and second scenes.


Click ▶ to see the project pause on each background image while the matching screen effect appears!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select a different sound for each scene by using music.melodyPlayable(music.Melody)?
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a sound effect for each scene!


Open Music, drag [play (to play) (playbackMode)] onto a blank line above the pause code for all 3 scenes. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


music.play(music.melodyPlayable(music.baDing), music.PlaybackMode.UntilDone)

Change the effect by deleting .baDing then retyping . after music to open the code completion tool of possible sounds. Scroll down the list to the properties then select one that fits the theme of each season.


Click ▶ to hear different sounds play for each season!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the code work as expected in blocks?

❓ What is something new that you can do in JavaScript, that you weren’t able to do when coding in blocks?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja make connections between the JavaScript text they have just written and their knowledge of blocks. Ninjas should be very familiar with these concepts already, so encourage them to think about the similarities and differences between blocks and text.
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how are the effects and dialog box parameters formatted in blocks, compared to JavaScript? How do the code comments appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?


Notice how the startScreenEffect functions turned into gray blocks. This is because they have special parameters that are not available in the blocks editor. This is just one example of how coding in JavaScript will provide more opportunities to customize code.

subgroups.introduction: Create a project with multiple scenes that tells something about different seasons in each scene!

validationItems.text: Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position.
Make the sprite move on its own and bounce on walls.
Use code comments and splash screens to create a title and 3 different scenes.
Use a screen effect with 2 parameters, 3 times.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about properties and code comments. In JavaScript, you can type directly on the editor to organize your code using code comments and set different sprite properties. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Parameter Pilot
badges.description: Use the JavaScript editor’s documentation and code completion tools when adding parameters to functions.

badges.title: Comment, Like, and Subscribe
badges.description: Add a comment to your code.

badges.title: Say What Now?
badges.description: Use the sayText function with all 5 parameters.

badges.title: Stop and Smell the Roses
badges.description: Use the pause function to temporarily stop your project from running new code.

badges.title: Effective Immediately
badges.description: Use the startScreenEffect function with 2 parameters.

badges.title: Music to My Ears
badges.description: Use the play function to play a melody.

badges.title: To Whom it May Concern
badges.description: Use the splash function to display a message on screen.

badges.title: A Speedy Recovery
badges.description: Set a sprite’s velocity property without using the setVelocity function.

badges.title: Wall of Text
badges.description: Use the showLongText function with 2 parameters.
